title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A transcription service allegedly recorded work meetings and used the recordings to train its AI systems without obtaining clear consent from all participants. The service's default settings enabled recording without requiring affirmative permission from meeting attendees, despite a privacy policy suggesting users consented by checking a box. The failure was in the deployment model: a system that captures audio from meetings was put into use without establishing that all parties to those conversations had knowingly agreed.

The core issue centers on consent for data use in training. The company's stated process for removing identifying information before training its AI was not clearly explained to users, making it unclear what protections actually existed between collection and model training. Catching this would have required either obtaining explicit informed consent from all meeting participants before any recording began, or implementing technical controls to prevent recording without active confirmation from everyone present.

It is not established whether the company intentionally designed the system to record without full consent, or whether recordings were actually used for training in the manner alleged.

Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed Friday accuses Otter.ai, a popular transcription service used for virtual meetings, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission and using them to train its artificial intelligence systems. The suit was brought by Justin Brewer of San Jacinto, California, who claims his privacy was severely violated. According to the complaint, Otter's software joins meetings and records participants by default without asking for consent from attendees, though the company's privacy policy states users grant permission when checking a box for training purposes. The lawsuit alleges that Otter violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws.

The case highlights growing privacy concerns about Otter, which now has approximately 25 million users worldwide and has recorded over 1 billion meetings since its founding in 2016. Recent complaints on social media describe incidents where Otter recorded sensitive business discussions and shared transcriptions with unintended parties. The lawsuit specifically questions the company's process for removing identifying information from recordings before using them in AI training, claiming the company provides no clear explanation of how it protects confidentiality. Otter maintains it does not share data with foreign governments or law enforcement agencies.
